Guest Information: The no_of_adults column depicts a minimum value of 0. This seems unusual for a hotel booking and might indicate data entry errors or specific booking types that need further investigation. Furthermore, the majority of bookings are for 2 adults (median and 75th percentile are 2).¶

The avg_price_per_room column has a minimum value of 0. This is highly unusual for a hotel booking, with the likelihood of indicating free stays or promotional bookings. It could be data errors that need to be addressed.¶

Special Requests: no_of_special_requests ranged from 0 to 5, with a mean of 0.61. This depicts that while many bookings have no special requests, some do.¶

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram

Observations on lead time¶

In [189]:
histogram_boxplot(data, "lead_time")

From the histogram and boxplot for 'lead_time', we can make the following observations:¶

The histogram indicates that the distribution of lead_time is highly right-skewed. This means that a large proportion of bookings are made with relatively short lead times, while a smaller number of bookings are made far in advance. The long tail extending to the right of the histogram represents those few bookings that occur much earlier than the majority.¶
In terms of central tendency, the histogram shows that the mean (represented by the green dashed line) is positioned significantly to the right of the median (represented by the black solid line). This pattern is typical of a right-skewed distribution and suggests that the average lead time is influenced by a small number of very large values. As a result, the mean lead time appears higher because it is pulled upward by bookings made far in advance.¶
The boxplot further supports the presence of right-skewness and illustrates the spread of the data. Numerous individual points appear beyond the upper whisker of the boxplot, indicating the presence of outliers. These outliers represent bookings that were made significantly earlier than most of the other reservations in the dataset.¶
The minimum value of the lead time is shown to be 0, as indicated by the lower whisker of the boxplot. This confirms that some reservations are made on the same day as the arrival date.¶
Additionally, the majority of bookings fall within the interquartile range (IQR) shown in the boxplot. Based on the descriptive statistics, the 25th percentile occurs at approximately 17 days, while the 75th percentile occurs at approximately 126 days. This indicates that most bookings are made between 17 and 126 days before arrival, highlighting the typical planning window for the majority of customers.¶

Finally, the interquartile range (IQR) displayed in the boxplot shows that the majority of the data is concentrated within a specific price range. # function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 2, 6))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 2, 6))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n],
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

Bivariate Analysis¶

In [205]:
cols_list = data.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()

plt.show()

From the heatmap showing the correlation matrix of the numerical features, we can observe that :¶

lead_time shows a positive correlation with booking_status. This suggests that bookings made further in advance are more likely to be canceled.¶
no_of_special_requests exhibits a negative correlation with booking_status. This implies that guests who make special requests are less likely to cancel their bookings, possibly because they are more invested in their stay.¶
no_of_previous_cancellations has a positive correlation with booking_status. This indicates that guests with a history of canceling previous bookings are more prone to canceling their current booking.¶
Repeated_guest shows a negative correlation with booking_status. Repeated guests are generally more reliable and less likely to cancel.¶
avg_price_per_room has a weak, likely positive, correlation with booking_status, suggesting that higher average prices might slightly increase the likelihood of cancellation, though this relationship is not strong.¶
Other variables like no_of_adults, no_of_children, no_of_weekend_nights, no_of_week_nights, required_car_parking_space, arrival_year, arrival_month, and arrival_date show relatively weak correlations with booking_status, indicating they might not be strong direct predictors of cancellation on their own.¶
no_of_adults and no_of_children have a weak positive correlation, which is expected as larger groups might include children.¶
no_of_previous_cancellations and no_of_previous_bookings_not_canceled show a negative correlation, meaning guests who frequently cancel tend to have fewer non-canceled bookings, and vice versa.¶
no_of_previous_bookings_not_canceled and repeated_guest have a strong positive correlation. This can be said to be logical, as repeated guests are more likely to have a history of non-canceled bookings.¶
no_of_week_nights and no_of_weekend_nights generally show a weak positive correlation.¶
There doesn't appear to be any extremely high correlation (e.g., >0.8 or < 0.8) among independent variables that would immediately suggest severe multicollinearity issues, but this would need a more detailed check if specific modeling techniques are employed.¶

We now want to Create functions that will help us with further analysis.¶

In [206]:
### function to plot distributions wrt target


def distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    target_uniq = data[target].unique()

    axs[0, 0].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[0]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[0, 1].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[1]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0])

    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot (without outliers) w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
In [207]:
def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 5, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

Data Preprocessing¶

Outlier Check¶

Let's check for outliers in the data.¶

In [225]:
# outlier detection using boxplot
numeric_columns = data.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()
# dropping booking_status
numeric_columns.remove("booking_status")

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 12))

for i, variable in enumerate(numeric_columns):
    plt.subplot(4, 4, i + 1)
    plt.boxplot(data[variable], whis=1.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.title(variable)

plt.show()

From the boxplots generated for the numerical columns, we can observe that :¶

Many of the numerical features exhibit a significant number of outliers, particularly on the upper side. This is visible as individual points extending far beyond the upper whiskers of the boxplots. Examples include lead_time, no_of_previous_cancellations, no_of_previous_bookings_not_canceled, and avg_price_per_room.¶
several features like lead_time, no_of_children, no_of_weekend_nights, no_of_week_nights, no_of_previous_cancellations, no_of_previous_bookings_not_canceled, and no_of_special_requests show strong right-skewness. This is indicated by the median being closer to the bottom of the box and long upper whiskers with many outliers.¶

Model Building¶

Model evaluation criterion¶

Model can make wrong predictions as:¶

Predicting a customer will not cancel their booking, but in reality, the customer will cancel their booking.¶
Predicting a customer will cancel their booking, but in reality, the customer will not cancel their booking.¶

In terms of this, which case is more important?¶

Both cases are important as:¶

If we predict that a booking will not be canceled and the booking gets canceled, then the hotel will lose resources and will have to bear additional costs of distribution channels.¶
If we predict that a booking will get canceled and the booking doesn't get canceled, the hotel might not be able to provide satisfactory services to the customer by assuming that this booking will be canceled. This might damage the brand equity.¶

How can the losses be reduced?¶

Hotel would want the F1 Score to be maximized, greater the F1 score higher the chances of minimizing False Negatives and False Positives.¶

First, let's create functions to calculate different metrics and confusion matrix so that we don't have to use the same code repeatedly for each model.¶

The model_performance_classification_statsmodels function will be used to check the model performance of models.¶

The confusion_matrix_statsmodels function will be used to plot the confusion matrix.¶

In [226]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using statsmodels
def model_performance_classification_statsmodels(
    model, predictors, target, threshold=0.5
):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    threshold: threshold for classifying the observation as class 1
    """

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred_temp = model.predict(predictors) > threshold
    # rounding off the above values to get classes
    pred = np.round(pred_temp)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf
In [227]:
# defining a function to plot the confusion_matrix of a classification model


def confusion_matrix_statsmodels(model, predictors, target, threshold=0.5):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    threshold: threshold for classifying the observation as class 1
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors) > threshold
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

This is a strong indicator of perfect multicollinearity. Variables like type_of_meal_plan_Meal Plan 3 and market_segment_type_Complementary have extremely large standard errors and insignificant p-values, making their coefficients highly unstable and unreliable. # we will define a function to check VIF
def checking_vif(predictors):
    vif = pd.DataFrame()
    vif["feature"] = predictors.columns

    # calculating VIF for each feature
    vif["VIF"] = [
        variance_inflation_factor(predictors.values, i)
        for i in range(len(predictors.columns))
    ]
    return vif

Dropping high p-value variables¶

We will drop the predictor variables having a p-value greater than 0.05 as they do not significantly impact the target variable.¶

But sometimes p-values change after dropping a variable. So, we'll not drop all variables at once.¶

Instead, we will do the following:¶

Build a model, check the p-values of the variables, and drop the column with the highest p-value.¶

Create a new model without the dropped feature, check the p-values of the variables, and drop the column with the highest p-value.¶

Repeat the above two steps till there are no columns with p-value > 0.05.¶

In [241]:
# initial list of columns
cols = X_train.columns.tolist()

# setting an initial max p-value
max_p_value = 1

while len(cols) > 0:
    # defining the train set
    x_train_aux = X_train[cols]

    # fitting the model
    model = sm.Logit(y_train, x_train_aux).fit(disp=False)

    # getting the p-values and the maximum p-value
    p_values = model.pvalues
    max_p_value = max(p_values)

    # name of the variable with maximum p-value
    feature_with_p_max = p_values.idxmax()

    if max_p_value > 0.05:
        cols.remove(feature_with_p_max)
    else:
        break

selected_features = cols
print(selected_features)

Converting coefficients to odds¶

The coefficients of the logistic regression model are in terms of log(odd), to find the odds we have to take the exponential of the coefficients.¶

Therefore, odds = exp(b)¶

The percentage change in odds is given as odds = (exp(b) - 1) * 100¶

From the calculated odds and percentage change in odds, we can make the following analysis for each predictor's impact on the likelihood of a booking being canceled, holding other variables constant:¶

Increased Likelihood of Cancellation (Positive Impact):¶
(arrival_year): For every one-unit increase in arrival year (e.g., from 2017 to 2018), the odds of cancellation increase by approximately 57.46%. This suggests that bookings in more recent years in this dataset had a higher tendency to cancel.¶
(no_of_previous_cancellations): A one-unit increase in previous cancellations increases the odds of current booking cancellation by approximately 25.67%. This confirms that guests with a history of cancellations are significantly more likely to cancel again.¶
(no_of_family_members): For each additional family member, the odds of cancellation increase by approximately 12.66%.¶
(no_of_weekend_nights): Each additional weekend night increases the odds of cancellation by about 11.45%.¶
(lead_time): For every one-unit increase in lead time (one more day in advance), the odds of cancellation increase by about 1.58%. This indicates that bookings made further in advance have a slightly higher chance of being canceled.¶
(avg_price_per_room): A one-unit increase in average price per room slightly increases the odds of cancellation by approximately 1.94%.¶
(no_of_week_nights): Each additional week night increases the odds of cancellation by about 4.27%.¶
'Meal Plan 2': Compared to the baseline meal plan, opting for 'Meal Plan 2' increases the odds of cancellation by approximately 17.77%.¶
Meal Plan 'Not Selected': If a meal plan is 'Not Selected', the odds of cancellation increase by approximately 32.63% compared to the baseline meal plan.¶
Decreased Likelihood of Cancellation (Negative Impact):¶
(repeated_guest): Being a repeated guest drastically reduces the odds of cancellation by about 93.51%. This is a very strong indicator of guest commitment.¶
Market Segment 'Offline': Bookings made through the 'Offline' market segment significantly decrease the odds of cancellation by approximately 83.25% compared to the baseline. This indicates higher commitment from offline channels.¶
(no_of_special_requests): For each additional special request, the odds of cancellation decrease by approximately 77.01%. This highlights that guests with special requests are highly committed.¶
'Room_Type 7': Reserving 'Room_Type 7' reduces the odds of cancellation by approximately 75.60% compared to the baseline room type.¶
'Room_Type 6': Reserving 'Room_Type 6' reduces the odds of cancellation by approximately 59.98%.¶

def plot_prec_recall_vs_tresh(precisions, recalls, thresholds):
    plt.plot(thresholds, precisions[:-1], "b--", label="precision")
    plt.plot(thresholds, recalls[:-1], "g--", label="recall")
    plt.xlabel("Threshold")
    plt.legend(loc="upper left")
    plt.ylim([0, 1])


plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))

The Precision-Recall curve plots Precision (y-axis) against Recall (x-axis) for different classification thresholds. It's particularly useful for imbalanced datasets, like our booking_status (cancellation) problem, where correctly identifying positive cases (cancellations) is crucial. A good model will have both high precision and high recall, meaning the curve will be closer to the top-right corner.¶
The shape of this curve indicates the model's ability to identify positive instances accurately. If the curve remains high for a large range of recall, it suggests a robust model. A steep drop in precision as recall increases would indicate that achieving high recall comes at a high cost of false positives. This curve complements the ROC curve by providing a more focused view on the performance of the minority class.¶

First, we will create functions to calculate different metrics and confusion matrix so that we don't have to use the same code repeatedly for each model.¶

The model_performance_classification_sklearn function will be used to check the model performance of models.¶

The confusion_matrix_sklearnfunction will be used to plot the confusion matrix.¶

In [265]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using sklearn
def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf
In [266]:
def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

min_samples_split min_samples_split: int or float, default=2

The minimum number of samples required to split an internal node:

- If int, then consider `min_samples_split` as the minimum number.
- If float, then `min_samples_split` is a fraction and
`ceil(min_samples_split * n_samples)` are the minimum
number of samples for each split.

.. versionchanged:: 0.18
Added float values for fractions. 		2
min_samples_leaf min_samples_leaf: int or float, default=1

The minimum number of samples required to be at a leaf node.
A split point at any depth will only be considered if it leaves at
least ``min_samples_leaf`` training samples in each of the left and
right branches. This may have the effect of smoothing the model,
especially in regression.

- If int, then consider `min_samples_leaf` as the minimum number.
- If float, then `min_samples_leaf` is a fraction and
`ceil(min_samples_leaf * n_samples)` are the minimum
number of samples for each node.

.. versionchanged:: 0.18
Added float values for fractions. 		1
min_weight_fraction_leaf min_weight_fraction_leaf: float, default=0.0

The minimum weighted fraction of the sum total of weights (of all
the input samples) required to be at a leaf node. Samples have
equal weight when sample_weight is not provided. 		0.0
max_features max_features: int, float or {"sqrt", "log2"}, default=None

The number of features to consider when looking for the best split:

- If int, then consider `max_features` features at each split.
- If float, then `max_features` is a fraction and
`max(1, int(max_features * n_features_in_))` features are considered at
each split.
- If "sqrt", then `max_features=sqrt(n_features)`.
- If "log2", then `max_features=log2(n_features)`.
- If None, then `max_features=n_features`.

.. note::

The search for a split does not stop until at least one
valid partition of the node samples is found, even if it requires to
effectively inspect more than ``max_features`` features. 		None
random_state random_state: int, RandomState instance or None, default=None

Controls the randomness of the estimator. The features are always
randomly permuted at each split, even if ``splitter`` is set to
``"best"``. When ``max_features < n_features``, the algorithm will
select ``max_features`` at random at each split before finding the best
split among them. But the best found split may vary across different
runs, even if ``max_features=n_features``. That is the case, if the
improvement of the criterion is identical for several splits and one
split has to be selected at random. To obtain a deterministic behaviour
during fitting, ``random_state`` has to be fixed to an integer.
See :term:`Glossary ` for details. 		1
max_leaf_nodes max_leaf_nodes: int, default=None

Grow a tree with ``max_leaf_nodes`` in best-first fashion.
Best nodes are defined as relative reduction in impurity.
If None then unlimited number of leaf nodes. 		None
min_impurity_decrease min_impurity_decrease: float, default=0.0

A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
greater than or equal to this value.

The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::

N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
- N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)

where ``N`` is the total number of samples, ``N_t`` is the number of
samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.

``N``, ``N_t``, ``N_t_R`` and ``N_t_L`` all refer to the weighted sum,
if ``sample_weight`` is passed.

.. versionadded:: 0.19 		0.0
class_weight class_weight: dict, list of dict or "balanced", default=None

Weights associated with classes in the form ``{class_label: weight}``.
If None, all classes are supposed to have weight one. For
multi-output problems, a list of dicts can be provided in the same
order as the columns of y.

Note that for multioutput (including multilabel) weights should be
defined for each class of every column in its own dict. For example,
for four-class multilabel classification weights should be
[{0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 5}, {0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 1}] instead of
[{1:1}, {2:5}, {3:1}, {4:1}].

The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
as ``n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))``

For multi-output, the weights of each column of y will be multiplied.

Note that these weights will be multiplied with sample_weight (passed
through the fit method) if sample_weight is specified. 		None
ccp_alpha ccp_alpha: non-negative float, default=0.0

Complexity parameter used for Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning. The
subtree with the largest cost complexity that is smaller than
``ccp_alpha`` will be chosen. By default, no pruning is performed. See
:ref:`minimal_cost_complexity_pruning` for details. See
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_tree_plot_cost_complexity_pruning.py`
for an example of such pruning.

.. versionadded:: 0.22 		0.0
monotonic_cst monotonic_cst: array-like of int of shape (n_features), default=None

Indicates the monotonicity constraint to enforce on each feature.
- 1: monotonic increase
- 0: no constraint
- -1: monotonic decrease

If monotonic_cst is None, no constraints are applied.

Monotonicity constraints are not supported for:
- multiclass classifications (i.e. when `n_classes > 2`),
- multioutput classifications (i.e. when `n_outputs_ > 1`),
- classifications trained on data with missing values.

The constraints hold over the probability of the positive class.

Read more in the :ref:`User Guide `.

.. versionadded:: 1.4 		None

Checking model performance on training set¶

In [268]:
# Plotting the confusion matrix for the training data
confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, X_train, y_train)
In [269]:
decision_tree_perf_train = model_performance_classification_sklearn(
    model, X_train, y_train
)
decision_tree_perf_train
Out[269]:
Accuracy Recall Precision F1
0 0.99421 0.98661 0.99578 0.99117

From the training performance output for the Decision Tree model, we can analyse that:¶

The model achieved a very high accuracy of approximately 99.42% on the training set. This suggests that the model is performing exceptionally well in classifying both canceled and non-canceled bookings in the data it was trained on.¶
The recall for the positive class (Canceled bookings) is about 98.66%. This means the model successfully identified almost all actual canceled bookings in the training data, indicating a very low number of false negatives.¶
The precision for canceled bookings is about 99.58%. This indicates that when the model predicts a booking will be canceled, it is correct nearly every time, resulting in a very low number of false positives.¶
The F1-score is approximately 99.12%. This extremely high F1-score, balancing both precision and recall, suggests excellent performance on the training data.¶
The metrics (Accuracy, Recall, Precision, F1-score) are all extremely high, nearing 100%. While this might seem ideal, such high performance on the training data is a strong indicator of overfitting for a Decision Tree model. This suggests that the model might have learned the training data too well, including its noise and specific patterns, and may not generalize as effectively to unseen data. It is crucial to evaluate this model's performance on the test set to confirm if it has learned generalizable patterns or merely memorized the training examples.¶

Checking model performance on test set¶

In [270]:
# Plotting the confusion matrix for the test data
confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, X_test, y_test)
In [271]:
# Checking performance on the test set
decision_tree_perf_test = model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, X_test, y_test)

# Displaying the performance metrics
decision_tree_perf_test
Out[271]:
Accuracy Recall Precision F1
0 0.86989 0.80863 0.79331 0.80090
The model achieved an accuracy of approximately 86.98% on the test set. This is a significant drop from the training accuracy (~99.42%), indicating some level of overfitting, but still a relatively good overall accuracy.¶
The recall for the positive class (Canceled bookings) is about 80.86%. This means the model correctly identified 80.86% of all actual canceled bookings in the unseen test data. This is a good recall score, meaning it's effective at minimizing false negatives.¶
The precision for canceled bookings is about 79.33%. This indicates that when the model predicts a booking will be canceled, it is correct 79.33% of the time on the test set.¶
The F1-score is approximately 80.09%. This balanced metric suggests a strong performance in identifying canceled bookings on unseen data, balancing both precision and recall.¶
Comparing these test set metrics (Accuracy: ~86.98%, Recall: ~80.86%, Precision: ~79.33%, F1: ~80.09%) to the training set metrics (Accuracy: ~99.42%, Recall: ~98.66%, Precision: ~99.58%, F1: ~99.12%), there is a clear drop in all performance metrics. This confirms the overfitting observed on the training data. While the test performance is still quite good, especially the F1-score of 80.09%, the model is not generalizing as perfectly as it did during training.¶
Further tuning (e.g., pruning the tree, setting max_depth, and min_samples_leaf) would likely be beneficial to reduce overfitting and potentially improve generalization even further.¶

Before pruning the tree let's check the important features.¶

In [272]:
feature_names = list(X_train.columns)
importances = model.feature_importances_
indices = np.argsort(importances)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))
plt.title("Feature Importances")
plt.barh(range(len(indices)), importances[indices], color="violet", align="center")
plt.yticks(range(len(indices)), [feature_names[i] for i in indices])
plt.xlabel("Relative Importance")
plt.show()

From the feature importances plot, we can analyze that:¶

The lead_time, avg_price_per_room, appear to be among the most influential features for the Decision Tree model in predicting booking status. These features have the longest bars, indicating higher relative importance.¶
Next Level of Importance: arrival_date,market_segment_type_Online, no_of_special_request and arrival_month¶
Many other features, particularly some of the room type or meal plan, and features like no_of_children have very low or even zero importance, suggesting they contribute little to the model's decision-making process in their current form.¶
This plot is very useful for pruning the tree. Features with very low importance might be candidates for removal, as they add complexity without much predictive power. Focusing on the most important features can help simplify the model, reduce overfitting, and potentially improve generalization.¶

Pruning the tree¶

Pre-Pruning¶

In [273]:
# Choose the type of classifier.
estimator = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1, class_weight="balanced")

# Grid of parameters to choose from
parameters = {
    "max_depth": np.arange(2, 7, 2),
    "max_leaf_nodes": [50, 75, 150, 250],
    "min_samples_split": [10, 30, 50, 70],
}

# Type of scoring used to compare parameter combinations
acc_scorer = make_scorer(f1_score)

# Run the grid search
grid_obj = GridSearchCV(estimator, parameters, scoring=acc_scorer, cv=5)
grid_obj = grid_obj.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Set the clf to the best combination of parameters
estimator = grid_obj.best_estimator_

# Fit the best algorithm to the data.
estimator.fit(X_train, y_train)

From the training performance output for the tuned Decision Tree model, we can analyze that:¶

The model achieved an accuracy of approximately 83.09% on the training set. This is a significant decrease from the untuned model's training accuracy (~99.42%), which is expected as pruning aims to reduce overfitting.¶
The recall for the positive class (Canceled bookings) is about 78.61%. This is lower than the untuned model's recall (~98.66%), but still a strong performance, indicating the model is good at identifying actual cancellations.¶
The precision for canceled bookings is about 72.42%. This is also lower than the untuned model's precision (~99.58%), reflecting the trade-off of reducing overfitting.¶
The F1-score is approximately 75.39%. This is a considerable drop from the untuned model's F1-score (~99.12%).¶
The decrease in all performance metrics on the training set compared to the untuned model indicates that the pruning (hyperparameter tuning) process was successful in reducing overfitting. While the scores are lower, this is a positive sign for generalization, as a less overfit model is expected to perform better on unseen data.¶
The next crucial step is to evaluate this tuned model's performance on the test set to confirm that it generalizes better.¶

From the test performance output for the tuned Decision Tree model, we can analyse that:¶

The model achieved an accuracy of approximately 83.50% on the test set. This is consistent with the training accuracy of the tuned model (~83.09%), suggesting good generalization, and it is a more realistic accuracy compared to the untuned model's overfitting.¶
The recall for the positive class (Canceled bookings) is about 78.34% on the test set. This indicates that the model is effectively identifying a high proportion of actual cancellations in unseen data.¶
The precision for canceled bookings is about 72.76% on the test set. This means that when the model predicts a booking will be canceled, it is correct about 72.76% of the time.¶
The F1-score is approximately 75.44%. This balanced metric suggests strong and stable performance in identifying canceled bookings on unseen data, balancing both precision and recall effectively.¶
Comparing these test set metrics (Accuracy: ~83.50%, Recall: ~78.34%, Precision: ~72.76%, F1: ~75.44%) to the training set metrics for the tuned model (Accuracy: ~83.09%, Recall: ~78.61%, Precision: ~72.42%, F1: ~75.39%), we observe that the performance is very consistent. This indicates that the pruning process was successful in reducing overfitting, and the tuned Decision Tree model generalizes well to unseen data. The F1-score of 75.44% on the test set is a robust indicator of the model's practical utility for predicting booking cancellations.¶

From the text report of the Decision Tree, we can analyze that:¶

This text report provides a precise, human-readable set of rules that the decision tree uses to classify bookings as 'Canceled' (1) or 'Not_Canceled' (0).¶
Each path from the root to a leaf represents a sequence of conditions (e.g., lead_time <= 151.50 AND no_of_special_requests <= 0.50) that, if met, lead to a specific class prediction (class: 0 for Not_Canceled, class: 1 for Canceled).¶
Feature Importance in Context: You can observe how different features (like lead_time, no_of_special_requests, market_segment_type_Online, avg_price_per_room, no_of_weekend_nights, arrival_month, no_of_week_nights, required_car_parking_space, type_of_meal_plan_Not Selected) are used at various nodes to make splits. Features closer to the top of the report (i.e., less indented) are generally more influential in the overall decision process.¶
Thresholds and Values: Each split condition clearly states the feature and the threshold value (e.g., lead_time <= 151.50, avg_price_per_room > 93.58).¶
This textual representation is excellent for interpreting why the model makes a certain prediction for a given input. You can trace the conditions that lead to a booking being classified as canceled or not canceled.¶

From the feature importances plot, we can analyze that:¶

The lead_time,market_segment_type_Online, and no_of_special_requests appear to be among the most influential features for the Decision Tree model in predicting booking status. These features have the longest bars, indicating higher relative importance.¶
average_price_per_room also contributes significantly.¶
Many other features, particularly some of the room type or meal plan, and features like no_of_children or arrival_date, have zero importance, suggesting they contribute little to the model's decision-making process in their current form.¶
This plot is very useful for pruning the tree. Features with very low importance might be candidates for removal, as they add complexity without much predictive power. Focusing on the most important features can help simplify the model, reduce overfitting, and potentially improve generalization.¶

Cost Complexity Pruning¶

Next, we train a decision tree using effective alphas. The last value in ccp_alphas is the alpha value that prunes the whole tree, leaving the tree, clfs[-1], with one node.¶

In [309]:
clfs = []
for ccp_alpha in ccp_alphas:
    clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(
        random_state=1, ccp_alpha=ccp_alpha, class_weight="balanced"
    )
    # Fitting the model on the training data
    clf.fit(X_train, y_train) 
    clfs.append(clf)

print(
    "Number of nodes in the last tree is: {} with ccp_alpha: {}".format(
        clfs[-1].tree_.node_count, ccp_alphas[-1]
    ))

Number of nodes in the last tree is: 3 with ccp_alpha: 0.03412090438134324

From the output, Number of nodes in the last tree is: 1 with ccp_alpha: 0.08117914389136927, we can analyze that:¶

The fact that the 'Number of nodes in the last tree is: 1' confirms that the largest ccp_alpha value in the ccp_alphas array (0.08117914389136927) effectively prunes the Decision Tree down to its simplest form, which is a single root node.¶
A single-node tree (or stump) essentially makes a prediction based solely on the majority class of the entire dataset (or the weighted majority if class_weight='balanced' is used). It has no splits and thus no predictive power beyond the base rate.¶
This step confirms that the ccp_alpha calculation successfully covered the entire pruning range, from a complex tree (corresponding to small ccp_alpha values) down to the simplest possible tree (corresponding to the largest ccp_alpha). The next step would typically involve evaluating trees along this path to find an optimal balance between complexity and generalization performance.¶
In [310]:
clfs = clfs[:-1]
ccp_alphas = ccp_alphas[:-1]

node_counts = [clf.tree_.node_count for clf in clfs]
depth = [clf.tree_.max_depth for clf in clfs]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7))
ax[0].plot(ccp_alphas, node_counts, marker="o", drawstyle="steps-post")
ax[0].set_xlabel("alpha")
ax[0].set_ylabel("number of nodes")
ax[0].set_title("Number of nodes vs alpha")
ax[1].plot(ccp_alphas, depth, marker="o", drawstyle="steps-post")
ax[1].set_xlabel("alpha")
ax[1].set_ylabel("depth of tree")
ax[1].set_title("Depth vs alpha")
fig.tight_layout()

From the test performance output for the post-pruning Decision Tree model, we can analyse that:¶

The model achieved an accuracy of approximately 86.87% on the test set. This is a very strong accuracy for unseen data and is consistent with the tuned model's training accuracy, suggesting good generalization.¶
The recall for the positive class (Canceled bookings) is about 85.83% on the test set. This indicates that the model is highly effective at identifying a large proportion of actual cancellations in unseen data, minimizing missed opportunities.¶
The precision for canceled bookings is about 76.47% on the test set. This means that when the model predicts a booking will be canceled, it is correct approximately 76.47% of the time.¶
The F1-score is approximately 80.88%. This balanced metric suggests strong and stable performance in identifying canceled bookings on unseen data, effectively balancing both precision and recall.¶
Comparing these test set metrics (Accuracy: ~86.87%, Recall: ~85.83%, Precision: ~76.47%, F1: ~80.88%) to the training set metrics for the post-pruning model (Accuracy: ~89.77%, Recall: ~90.24%, Precision: ~80.91%, F1: ~85.32%), we observe that the performance is very consistent. This indicates that the cost-complexity pruning was highly successful in reducing overfitting, and the Decision Tree model generalizes exceptionally well to unseen data.¶
The F1-score of 80.88% on the test set is a robust indicator of the model's practical utility for predicting booking cancellations in a real-world scenario.¶

This plot helps in understanding which aspects of the booking information are most critical for the pruned Decision Tree to determine the booking_status. The consistency of top features between the untuned and pruned tree suggests their fundamental importance, while the overall reduction in total features contributes to a more interpretable and potentially more generalizable model.¶

Let's compare the training and test performance for all Decision Tree models:¶

Training Performance Comparison (F1-score):¶

Decision Tree (untuned): 0.99117¶
Decision Tree (Pre-Pruning): 0.75386¶
Decision Tree (Post-Pruning): 0.85320¶

Test Performance Comparison (F1-score):¶

Decision Tree (untuned): 0.80090¶
Decision Tree (Pre-Pruning): 0.75444¶
Decision Tree (Post-Pruning): 0.80883¶

Analysis:¶

Untuned Decision Tree: This model shows a very high F1-score on the training set (0.99117) but a significantly lower F1-score on the test set (0.80090). This large drop indicates severe overfitting to the training data. While its test F1-score is still relatively good, the large discrepancy suggests it learned noise and specific patterns from the training data that do not generalize well.¶
Decision Tree (Pre-Pruning): This model shows a training F1-score of 0.75386 and a test F1-score of 0.75444. The scores are very consistent, indicating good generalization and no overfitting. However, the overall F1-score is lower than the other models, suggesting it might be too simple and potentially underfitting or not capturing enough complexity from the data.¶
Decision Tree (Post-Pruning): This model achieved an F1-score of 0.85320 on the training set and 0.80883 on the test set. While there is a slight drop from training to test, it's a much smaller gap compared to the untuned model. More importantly, its test F1-score (0.80883) is the highest among all Decision Tree models. This indicates that cost-complexity pruning was highly effective in finding a model that generalizes very well to unseen data, balancing complexity and predictive power.¶

In conclusion:¶

The Decision Tree (Post-Pruning) model is the best-performing Decision Tree model, achieving the highest F1-score of 0.80883 on the unseen test data. It successfully addresses the overfitting issue seen in the untuned model while maintaining a strong predictive capability.¶

Conclusion¶

Based on the comprehensive exploratory data analysis, and the development of both Logistic Regression and Decision Tree models, here are the conclusions and INN Hotels Group:¶

Overall Best Model: The Decision Tree (Post-Pruning) model emerged as the superior choice for predicting booking cancellations. It achieved the highest F1-score of 0.80883 on the unseen test data, significantly outperforming the Logistic Regression model's best F1-score of 0.70018. This indicates that the Decision Tree model provides a more effective balance between identifying actual cancellations (recall) and minimizing false alarms (precision), while also demonstrating good generalization capability after cost-complexity pruning.¶

Several factors consistently influence the likelihood of booking cancellations:¶

Lead_Time: Bookings made further in advance show a higher probability of cancellation, and also a critical factor. This was a consistently strong predictor across both models. Guests who book far in advance were statistically more likely to cancel.¶
Average Price per Room: Bookings with higher average prices per room were slightly more likely to be canceled. That is to say, higher room rates correlate with a higher probability of cancellation in certain segments.¶
Market Segment Type: 'Online' bookings also generally had a higher cancellation rate compared to 'Corporate' and 'Offline' segments.¶
No. of Special Requests: Guests who made special requests (especially multiple requests) showed signs significantly likely to cancel. •¶
Arrival_Month and arrival_date exhibited some form of cancellation rate, but can not be compared to other to ealier factors.¶

Decreased Cancellation Risk Factors ( with a higher Commitment): -¶

Repeated Guests showed a highly reliability with an extremely low cancellation rate.¶

Actionable Recommendations for INN Hotels Group:¶

Based on these findings, the following strategies are recommended:¶

The trained Decision Tree model can be utilized to proactively identify bookings that have a high likelihood of cancellation. This enables the hotel management to implement strategic interventions before cancellations occur. Furthermore, the interpretable nature of the Decision Tree model allows hotel staff to easily understand the underlying rules and factors that contribute to a booking being classified as high-risk, thereby supporting more informed decision-making.¶
For bookings identified as high-risk (for example, those with long lead times and no special requests), the hotel can implement automated and personalized re-confirmation messages or phone calls closer to the scheduled arrival date. This approach can help remind guests of their reservations, encourage commitment to the booking, and potentially reduce the likelihood of cancellations.¶
The hotel should further invest in and actively promote loyalty programs aimed at repeat guests. Given their exceptionally high reliability and very low cancellation rates, these customers represent a highly valuable segment. By offering personalized promotions, exclusive benefits, and tailored services, the hotel can strengthen customer relationships and encourage continued patronage from this loyal group.¶
The hotel should review and refine its pricing strategies for long-stay and high-value bookings to better manage cancellation risks and optimize revenue. One approach is to introduce tiered cancellation policies based on factors such as lead time and length of stay, allowing more flexible terms for low-risk bookings while applying stricter conditions to higher-risk reservations.¶
Additionally, the hotel may consider implementing small non-refundable deposits or offering discounted non-refundable booking rates for high-risk customer segments. These measures can help secure guest commitment and reduce the likelihood of cancellations.¶
Hotels should actively encourage guests to include special requests during the booking process. These requests can provide valuable insights into guest preferences and needs. Ensuring that such requests are effectively addressed can enhance guest satisfaction and strengthen their commitment to the reservation. Additionally, the presence of special requests may serve as an indicator of a highly committed guest, making it an important factor to consider in booking management and customer relationship strategies.¶
Hotels should adjust their operational planning and marketing strategies in response to seasonal booking trends. During periods characterized by higher cancellation rates, the hotel can implement more proactive re-confirmation campaigns and carefully apply overbooking strategies to maintain optimal occupancy levels. Conversely, during months with lower demand and fewer cancellations, management should focus on attracting new customers and promoting longer stays through value-added packages and promotional offers.¶
The hotel should also develop tailored strategies for different market segments. By understanding the booking behaviors, preferences, and cancellation patterns associated with each segment, management can design targeted marketing initiatives, pricing strategies, and service offerings that better meet the needs of each group while improving overall booking stability and revenue performance.¶
For online bookings, the hotel should consider offering exclusive incentives for guests who book directly through the hotel’s official channels. Providing benefits such as discounted rates, complimentary services, or flexible booking options can encourage direct bookings and reduce reliance on third-party platforms, which may be associated with higher cancellation rates. Additionally, the hotel should focus on strengthening relationships with corporate clients, as this segment often demonstrates higher reliability and lower cancellation tendencies. Developing long-term partnerships, offering corporate packages, and providing tailored services for business travelers can help maintain a stable and consistent stream of bookings.¶
The performance of the predictive model should be continuously monitored to ensure its effectiveness over time. Regular evaluation and periodic retraining of the model using updated data are essential to maintain its accuracy and reliability. This is particularly important because booking behaviors and market conditions may evolve over time, which can influence cancellation patterns and overall model performance.¶
